title: Welcome to the Labeeba Digital Journal
summary: A quick note on what this space is for, and what's coming as we build out the site.
content: This journal is where we'll document the systems we build for clients, along with the odd behind-the-scenes post about how the site itself was put together. Over the next few posts I'm walking through the JavaScript layer added to this site in Phase 2 -- a theme switcher, a dynamically loaded header and footer, this very blog section, contact form validation, and a live filter on the Work page. Each post covers what the feature does, how I approached building it, what tripped me up along the way, and what I'd do differently next time.

title: Building the Dark/Light Theme Switcher
summary: How the toggle in the nav remembers your theme choice across every page, using localStorage and CSS custom properties.
content: The theme switcher toggles a data-theme attribute on the body element, which flips a set of CSS custom properties defined in style.css -- the dark palette lives in :root as the default, and a body[data-theme='light'] rule overrides the same variable names with light-mode values. Because every color in the stylesheet is written as var(--something) instead of a hard-coded hex, the whole page repaints correctly the instant the attribute changes, without touching a single other CSS rule. The trickiest part wasn't the toggle itself -- it was persistence. localStorage.setItem('theme', theme) makes the choice stick across a reload, and on every page load a small check runs before anything else to read that saved value and apply it immediately, which avoids a flash of the wrong theme. The real complication showed up once Part 2 moved the toggle button itself into a dynamically loaded header: the button doesn't exist in the DOM at the moment the page first loads, so the click listener can't be attached on DOMContentLoaded like the starter code assumed. I split the logic in two -- the theme is applied to <body> immediately regardless of whether the button exists yet, and a separate initThemeToggle() function gets exposed on window and called by components.js right after the header markup is injected. If I were redoing this, I'd probably store theme state in a tiny shared module instead of a global function, but for a project this size it does the job cleanly.

title: Wiring Up the Journal to a JSON File
summary: Why this page you're reading right now isn't hard-coded HTML -- it's rendered from data/posts.json on every load.
content: Before this post existed as data, the Journal page was just static markup -- three placeholder cards typed directly into blog.html. Phase 3 replaced that with a fetch('data/posts.json') call that pulls every post as a plain object with an id, title, date, summary, category, and content field, sorts them newest-first by date, and builds a post-card for each one. The newest post also gets a small 'Latest Post' badge, which just checks whether its index in the sorted array is 0. Getting the date formatting right took a couple of tries -- new Date('2025-05-15') parses as UTC midnight, which can quietly roll over to the previous day depending on the reader's timezone, so I append T00:00:00 before parsing to force it to local time. The other small design decision was adding a Read More toggle that reveals the full content field instead of dumping every post's full text onto the page at once; it also had to work fine even though the cards themselves don't exist until after the fetch resolves, which meant any script depending on this content (like the filter box) needs to be re-run afterward rather than assumed to already have found everything on page load.

title: Contact Form Validation, Without a Framework
summary: Inline error messages, a live character count for the message field, and a success state -- all in plain JavaScript.
content: The contact form validates three things before it's allowed to 'submit': the name field can't be empty, the email field has to match a basic email pattern, and the message field needs at least 20 characters. Each field has a small span.error-msg sitting right beneath it in the markup, hidden by default, and a showError/clearError pair of functions handles toggling a 'visible' class on that span along with an 'invalid' class on the input itself for the red border. The part I underestimated was how much better the form feels with errors clearing in real time -- each field has its own input event listener that wipes its error the moment the user starts correcting it, instead of making them wait for another failed submit to find out they fixed it. Once every field passes, the form itself gets hidden and a success message takes its place, which was a simple swap but makes the whole interaction feel finished instead of just silently doing nothing. The email regex is intentionally basic (something@something.something) rather than a fully RFC-compliant pattern -- for a contact form, catching obvious typos matters more than technically valid edge cases nobody actually types.

title: One Filter Script, Two Different Pages
summary: How the same filter.js file powers live search on both the Work page and this Journal, including posts that don't exist yet when the page loads.
content: The brief asked for a live filter on both the Work page and the Journal page, and my first instinct was to write two versions -- one for product cards, one for post cards. Instead, filter.js reads three data attributes off the search input itself (data-card-selector, data-title-selector, data-category-selector), so the exact same script can filter completely different markup on each page just by changing what's in the HTML, not the JavaScript. The genuinely tricky part was the Journal page specifically: its cards don't exist in the DOM until blog.js finishes its fetch, which happens after the filter's input listener has already been attached. Rather than reaching for MutationObserver or manual event delegation, I just made the filter function re-query the DOM with querySelectorAll on every keystroke instead of caching a card list once -- so it naturally picks up cards that show up later. I also exposed the filter's run function on window.reapplyFilter so blog.js can call it once directly after rendering, in case someone had already typed a search term before the posts finished loading. It's a small trick, but it meant zero special-casing between the two pages.
